title: Seeking Cost-Optimal Infrastructure Size for Distributed Filesystems: A Ceph Case Study
problem: Predicting distributed filesystem I/O performance based solely on hardware configuration is not straightforward
motivation: Cost-effective DFS design requires understanding how hardware choices (cores, RAM, bandwidth) affect actual performance
method: They tested Ceph, a distributed storage system, by systematically changing how much CPU, memory, and disk bandwidth it could access. Using Linux hotplug (which dynamically enables or disables CPU cores) and Cgroups (which constrains how many resources a process can use), they created different hardware configurations. They then measured I/O performance—how fast the system could read and write data—under each configuration.
key_novelty: Adding more CPU, memory, or disk bandwidth to a distributed filesystem doesn't speed up I/O performance proportionally; the relationship is non-linear and depends on which resource is increased.
contributions: Method for assessing hardware configuration impact on DFS
Evidence that resource reduction doesn't yield proportional performance loss
